english: Consider the differential equation $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2y$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$, whose general solution is usually written as $y=cx^{2}$, $c\in\mathbb{R}$. Which of the following functions $y:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$, satisfies the equation at every $x\in\mathbb{R}$, and is not of the form $y=cx^{2}$ for any single constant $c$?
hindi: अवकल समीकरण $x\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2y$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$ पर विचार कीजिए, जिसका व्यापक हल प्रायः $y=cx^{2}$, $c\in\mathbb{R}$ के रूप में लिखा जाता है। निम्न में से कौन-सा फलन $y:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $\mathbb{R}$ पर अवकलनीय है, प्रत्येक $x\in\mathbb{R}$ पर समीकरण को संतुष्ट करता है, तथा किसी भी एक अचर $c$ के लिए $y=cx^{2}$ के रूप का नहीं है?
solution: On $(0,\infty)$ and on $(-\infty,0)$ separately the solutions are $y=c_1x^{2}$ and $y=c_2x^{2}$; at $x=0$ the equation only needs $y(0)=0$
(A): each piece satisfies $xy'=2y$; both one-sided derivatives at $0$ are $0$, so $y$ is differentiable and $0\cdot y'(0)=0=2y(0)$; $c_1=1\neq c_2=-2$, so not of the form $cx^{2}$
(B) is a solution but is of the form $cx^{2}$
(C): for $x<0$, $x(2x+1)=2x^{2}+x\neq 2(x^{2}+x)$; also the left derivative at $0$ is $1\neq0$
solution_full: Separating variables, $\dfrac{dy}{y}=\dfrac{2\,dx}{x}$ on any interval not containing $0$ (where $y\neq0$), so on $(0,\infty)$ every solution is $y=c_1x^{2}$ and on $(-\infty,0)$ every solution is $y=c_2x^{2}$ (the zero function is included as $c=0$).

At $x=0$ the equation reads $0\cdot y'(0)=2y(0)$, so it only requires $y(0)=0$, which both pieces give. A function made of $c_1x^{2}$ for $x\ge0$ and $c_2x^{2}$ for $x<0$ has right derivative $0$ and left derivative $0$ at the origin, so it is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$. Hence the full set of solutions on $\mathbb{R}$ is a two-parameter set, larger than the one-parameter family $y=cx^{2}$.

(A) is this construction with $c_1=1$, $c_2=-2$. It satisfies the equation for every $x$ and is differentiable at $0$. Since $c_1\neq c_2$, no single $c$ gives it. So (A) satisfies all three conditions.
(B) $y=3x^{2}$ is a solution, but it is $cx^{2}$ with $c=3$, so it fails the last condition.

(C) For $x<0$: $xy'=x(2x+1)=2x^{2}+x$ while $2y=2x^{2}+2x$; these differ, so the equation fails. Moreover the left derivative at $0$ is $1$ and the right derivative is $0$, so it is not differentiable at $0$.
(D) For $x>0$: $y=x^{3}$, $xy'=3x^{3}\neq 2x^{3}=2y$, so it is not a solution.
originality_note: New: the general solution of xy' = 2y, obtained on each half-line, does not cover all solutions on R because the equation degenerates at x = 0; the question asks which function is a genuine solution outside the family. Closest known: questions asking which function is a solution of a given DE. Different because: the student must check differentiability at the singular point x = 0 and see that the solution set on R is two-parameter.
blueprint_concepts: General vs particular solution; verifying a solution

concept_use.General vs particular solution; verifyin: The usual general solution y = cx^2 is shown not to contain every solution on R: the solution set on R is two-parameter, and option (A) is a solution that no single c gives; (B) is a solution that is a particular case of the general solution.

stem_review: Read as a student: every symbol and function introduced with its domain, conditions complete, one reading of each sentence; answer recomputed with sympy and unique; the phrase 'not of the form cx^2 for any single constant c' has one reading; only (A) meets all three conditions (B is a solution but of the form; C and D fail the equation). Web search found lecture notes on pasting solutions of this equation, not this question. Changed: No change.
key_step: Solutions on each side of 0 are independent multiples of x^2; pasting them is differentiable at 0.
justification: Needs the idea that the singular point x = 0 lets the constants differ on the two sides, plus a differentiability check; a conceptual step but short. Comparable to 2021-P2-Q4 (L3), which also asks which functions belong to a solution family, but this is a single check, so L2.
